messages.subject: binomial models with varying, including zero, number of trials
messages.subject_clean: binomial models with varying, including zero, number of trials
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to use INLA to model disease treatments in different areas over time.

The data are the number of cases of disease, and the number of treatments for that disease in each area in each time period. The main thing I'm interested in is the probability of treatment in any given area, so it seems obvious that I would model the number of treatments as being a binomial process with number cases known and some underlying unknown probability (to be estimated), dependant on the area and time period.

Unfortunately, some of the areas have no cases for some time periods, and therefore also no treatments. However, I can't just throw these away, since there is still some underlying probability of treatment, were there to be a case, and presumably also of there being some cases.

This paper sets out better than I why these zeros are of interest, and some ways to deal with them: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2843591/. The summary is to model the cases and treatments as two poisson processes that are correlated.

This paper uses INLA to model a poisson process and then a binomial process that depends on the number of trials in the poisson process: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210x.12017/abstract. It is also very similar to the toy example http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools#TOC-Models-with-more-than-one-type-of-likelihood. However, in both these cases none of the instances have zero trials.

My example looks something like this:

n=100
area = rep(1:10, each=10)
time = rep.int <http://rep.int>(1:10, 10)
cases = rpois(n, 4)
treatments = round(0.5*cases, 0)

data <- data.frame(area, time, cases, treatments)

formula <- treatments~1+f(area) #ignoring the time variable for now

result <- inla(formula, family="binomial", data=data, Ntrials=cases)

And it produces error:

*** ERROR ***  INLA.Data1: Binomial data[33] (nb,y) = (0,0) is void

because it can't handle having instances of zero cases. I've also tried putting it into the form of the Illian paper, but the same error appears. Can you suggest how I can achieve something like the Scott Comulada model, or adapt the Illian model to my uses. Or, which is quite likely, can you suggest a better way than either?

Thank you,

Duncan

On 3 October 2013 19:30, xiao guo <xiao.g...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> 1. inla.mesh.fem(mesh, order = 2) : what I understand is that 'order=2' here is the \alpha = 2 in the SPDE
> (\kappa^2-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}x(u) = W(u),
> not the order of the basis functions psi_j , j = 1... n.  Yes?

Correct.

> If so, I guess that if I want higher order basis functions, I have  to modify the code where the FE matrices c0 c1 g1  g2 ... are calculated.

Yes, or rather calculate them elsewhere, in R, since that is probably
easier than directly adding to the existing C++ code.  More on that
below.

> 2. inla.mesh.fem gives some matrices
> c0[i,j] = < psi_i, 1 >
> c1[i,j] = < psi_i, psi_j >
> g1[i,j] = < grad psi_i, grad psi_j >
> g2 = g1 * c0^-1 * g1

For gk there's a misprint in the documentation.  It should say this instead:

  gk = g1 * (c0^-1 * g1)^(k-1), up to and including k=order

> c0 c1 g1 should be \tilde{C}, C, G in Lindgren et al. (2011).

Yes.

> But what is g2 (...gk)?
> It looks like Q_{2,\kappa^2} =  K_{\kappa^2}*C^{-1}*K_{\kappa^2} in Result 2 of Lindgren et al. (2011) but not, since g1 is not "K_{\kappa^2} =\kappa^2*C+G".

c0/c1, g1, g2, g3, etc are the matrices that appear when expanding the
"K C^-1 K" expression into a polynomial in "kappa".  For alpha=2,
Q = tau^2(kappa^4 C + 2 kappa^2 G + G C^-1 G)
which is represented as
Q = tau^2(kappa^4 c0 + 2 kappa^2 g1 + g2)

> 3. In inla.mesh.fem, it seems to call another function 'inla.fmesher.smorg' to calculate the matrices where however I can not find explicit steps for the calculation. It calls some functions such as fmesher.write, inla.affirm.double, inla.fmesher.make.prefix, that even have no help documentation... Could you please show me where can I find the steps for calculating <psi_i, psi_j> , <grad psi_i, grad psi_j>, etc .. ?

The actual calculations are done in the standalone executable
"fmesher", which deals with mesh generation, locating points in
triangulated meshes, fem matrix construction, etc.  You can see the
C++ code via the INLA Google Code repository, direct link
  http://code.google.com/p/inla/source/browse/#hg%2Ffmesher%2Fsrc

For 1d models, the   inla.mesh.1d.fem()  does calculate the needed
matrices in R, using (exact) Gaussian quadrature.

> 4. Could you please explain what are the matrices in spde$param.inla$, such as M0 M1 M2 B0 B1 B2? I looked at the help doc for this, but could not link these to those matrices in your paper (denoted by C,G,K,Q ... ) so that I am confused with the meaning of these matrices and their utility here.

Those matrices describe the internal model representation as seen by
the inla program; to use different c0/1, g1, g2, etc, matrices, you
don't actually need to know about the details for that, but should
instead look at how inla.spde.matern() uses it's matrices, since you'd
need to do exactly the same, replacing only the inla.mesh.fem()
output.  (Actually, it's more complicated than that since with higher
order basis functions the number of basis functions doesn't match the
number of triangles, so one has to be very careful, but the 1d models
already deal with it)
The B-matrices from the point of view of the user are essentially
described in the help for inla.spde2.matern(), but better in the
tutorial
http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial-from-jss

The B-matrices for inla.spde2.generic are not always the same as for
inla.spde2.matern, since they refer to the internal representation.  I
can send you the design document.

Further discussion of this would be better off-list, since it's highly
technical and depending on implementation details that are subject to
change.

Finn

Hi,

I explained some more details directly to Duncan, but in summary, for
the benefit of the list:

Solution 1) Extend the INLA Binomial model to support the degenerate
deterministic "Bin(0, p)" model, where the parameter "p" has no
influence, as all realisations are necessarily =0.  This requires some
small changes to the current inla code.

Solution 2) Remove the observations where cases==0.

messages.subject_clean: Smoothing in one spatial and one temporal dimension with SPDE
messages.body_plain:
I've got about 12000 observations at a 5 second frequency from some aerosol equipment that's moving back and forth across a line in space. I'm interested in fitting a spatio-temporal model to examine how the spatial trend changes with time. I managed to fit an SPDE model to the data based on the Leukemia example but I don't feel comfortable using this approach as the smoothing in space and in time shouldn't be the same (apples to oranges).

The spatial component of the data has about 2500 unique observation locations, but they're not on a regularly spaced mesh (the equipment moves back and forth with slightly different speeds each time, as it's being carried by a person). The observations are dense in both space and time and there are immobile observation points in space so we can identify spatial and temporal variation.

I've tried fitting a model using JAGS that sets up a tensor P-spline basis (Brezger and Lang, 2004) but the graph is of size tens of millions for the full data set. It segfaults on my university's supercomputer but it can run on a subset of the data (1000). The precision matrix for the prior for the spline parameters is then \lambda_1 Q_1 + \lambda_2 Q_2 where Q_1 and Q_2 are the kronecker products of the univariate smoothing penalties (as in the rw2 model) and the identity matrix.

Is there a way of using inla.spde.generic to do the appropriate smoothing so that we're smoothing in space and in time while having a mesh basis?

Is this 2d space + 1d time or 1+1?

If its the first, it should run with the Cameletti stuff (although there'll be a limit to the resolution you can fit). If its the second, you can still use the Cameletti stuff grouping with a 1d instead of a 2d model.

As far as I can see, the model you've proposed fits space and time the same way (with different variances), so im not sure how appropriate it is. (In maths models, the time derivative always has a different sign, so this is like fitting an anisotropic Matern model, which may well work but I'm not sure.)

For INLA.spde.generic for this model, you want to set M0=Q1, M1=0 and M2=Q2. This will fit the model
Phi1*Phi2*Q1 + Phi1*Q2,

WHere log(Phi1)=B0*THETA and log(Phi2)=B1*THETA and THETA~ N(mu,Q^{-1}). Note that this notation is a bit bad because first value of the B matrices are offsets. See the tutorials that admin has written for decent notation(sorry). For the correct values of B0 and B1 you can get your model.

I'm a touch worried about the resolution still - 10million nodes for only 12k observations seems a bit excessive. If you want that sort of resolution, you'll have to roll your own (I don't think any existing code can touch a problem that size)

Best wishes,

Dan

On Fri, 2013-10-11 at 11:25 -0700, SW wrote:
> Is there a way to specify linear combination for a model with factor
> covariates? I am faced with the error below when trying to do linear
> combination with my age group covariate. My work-around right now is
> to define multiple dummy variables for each age group, then use these
> dummy variables (as numeric) in the model. This gets very tedious,
> however, as I have multiple categorical variables that will need to be
> put into the model.

for

	formula = y ~ x

where 'x' is a factor, then the model.matrix() function expands this
into a sum of indicator variables, one for each level. Not all levels
needs to be presented, as this also depends on the contents of 'x'. (see
also a FAQ entry on this with R (and ?control.fixed)

the consequence, is that the expanded variable names need to be used
when defining a linear combination.

> x = as.factor(c("a", "b", 2))
> x
[1] a b 2
Levels: 2 a b
> r = inla(y ~ x, data = data.frame(y=1:3,x))
> rownames(r$summary.fixed)
[1] "(Intercept)" "xa"          "xb"

so we need to do

> r = inla(y ~ x, data = data.frame(y=1:3,x), lincomb =
inla.make.lincomb(xa=-1,xb=1))

--

Currently, changing M* in param.inla of the spde-object will not have
the desired effect in inla() unless you also write those matrices to
disk in the appropriate way, and an easier approach is to use
inla.spde2.generic() instead to setup you model.  However, both
approaches require that the resulting model gives positive definite
precision matrices.

disk) will still allow the functions implemented in R to work with the
object:

eigenvalues with

theta-combinations.  If they aren't, then you M*-matrices do not
generate a valid model.

Hi Thordis!

You're mixing two separate issues here:
1) that predictions get more uncertain with longer lead times is a
direct effect from calculating conditional distributions into the
future, which will automatically have increasing variances.
2) What you seem to be asking about is that you also want increasing
uncertainty due to uncertainty about changes in the model itself.

Issue 1) is automatic, and issue 2) can be done in at least one way:
For 1D spde models (which includes AR(1) and AR(2)-like models), one can
specify a log-linear model for the spde parameters, such as the
variance, allowing for temporal trends in the model parameters, or
seasonal parameter variation based on seasonal covariates.

Finn

INLA gives you the predictive distribution for the linear predictor in
the model.  If you want the predictive distribution for potential
observations from the observation model that needs to be integrated
separately (except for some special cases where the model can be written
on a form that allows inla to do that integration as well) as that in
general can be both discrete and/or otherwise non-Gaussian.

> prediction, but the predictive distribution is seriously underdispersive
> as the variance of the likelihood model is not accounted for.

Well, yes, it the correct predictive distribution for a _different_
latent variable than you unobserved future observations, so the coverage
_shouldn't_ match.

> That is, I
> need to do something like the following

<cut>

> This gives me a coverage of approximately 80% for the 80% prediction
> interval. If I only look at the quantiles of the distribution in
> summary.fitted.values, I get a coverage of about 20% as that is not the
> predictive distribution for the missing variable Y[n].

Yes, "fitted.values" refers to the link-function-transformed linear
predictor, so is not comparable to observations (it describes a
parameter, which is usually an expectation, so it may appear to be on
the same scale as the observations, but it doesn't include the
observational variability at all).

There are several functions to produce posterior samples, e.g.
inla.posterior.sample(), which produces predictive samples from
the latent variables and model parameters, which can then be combined
with sampling from the observation likelihood models.  This is currently
the only completely general method I know of for doing observation-scale
predictive distributions with INLA.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit the following non-parametric spatio-temporal disease mapping model:

O_it|r_it ~ Poisson(E_it*r_it)

log(r_it) = alpha + u_i + v_i + gamma_t + phi_t + delta_it    for i=1,...,I and t=1,...,T

Using a completely structured TypeIV space-time interaction (Knorr-Held, 2000),
the structure matrix for the interaction (R_delta = R_u x R_gamma) has a rank deficiency of I+T-1 if gamma follows a RW1.

According to Schödle and Held (2011), "to ensure identifiability of interaction term delta, specific sum-to-zero constraints have to be used".

My data have I=501 areas and T=23 years, so I have to specify the following linear constraints

A*delta=e, where A is a 523 x 11523 matrix.

The problem is that when I run the model in INLA (even with the "gaussian" strategy), this error message appears:
"This application has requested the Runtime to terminate it in an unusual way."

The model is well fitted when I use a TypeI or TypeIII interaction, so I think that the problem is the high number of linear constraints.

Is there any way to solve this problem?

Thank you very much,
Aritz.
